extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners / attorneys and disciplinary adjudicators (USPTO OED, bar counsel)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria applied in disciplinary proceedings against a registered patent practitioner for unauthorized practice of law and related professional misconduct, focusing on USPTO ethical rules and applicable federal/state court admission rules (pro hac vice, local rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Local Rule 83.5.3(b) pro hac vice prerequisites
rubrics_metrics.description: Local Rule 83.5.3(b) expressly requires an attorney wishing to 'appear and practice' before the district court to file and certify that (1) he is a member of the bar in good standing in every jurisdiction where he is admitted to practice; (2) no disciplinary proceedings are pending against him; and (3) he is familiar with the Local Rules and a member of the district court’s bar has appeared and moved for his admission. Further, until the attorney’s application is granted, he 'may not enter an appearance or sign any papers' submitted to the district court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The local rule grants the court discretion in deciding motions to appear pro hac vice and is grounded in 28 U.S.C. § 1654 and Fed. R. Civ. P. 83. Compliance with state ethics rules (e.g., Mass. R. Prof’l Conduct 5.5) does not substitute for satisfying the district court’s local rules. The filing/signing of pleadings by an attorney who has not satisfied these prerequisites constitutes an unauthorized appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing or signing pleadings constitutes appearance (LR 83.5.2(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: The filing of the complaint shall constitute an appearance by the attorney who signs it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An attorney cannot avoid the appearance requirement by withholding his signature or having a pro se client sign if the attorney drafted and substantially prepared the document. Notation that a document was 'prepared with the aid of' an attorney does not negate that the attorney practiced if he drafted/orchestrated the litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'practice of law' (Massachusetts standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice of law includes directing and managing the enforcement of legal claims and the establishment of the legal rights of others, where it is necessary to form and to act upon opinions as to what those rights are and as to the legal methods which must be adopted to enforce them, the practice of giving or furnishing legal advice as to such rights and methods and the practice, as an occupation, of drafting documents by which such rights are created, modified, surrendered or secured (quoting In re Hrones).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crafting a sophisticated civil rights lawsuit, causing commencement and directing prosecution of the lawsuit, and drafting pleadings that create or modify rights all fall within this definition and therefore constitute practicing law in Massachusetts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mass. R. Prof’l Conduct 5.5: temporary services limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass. R. Prof’l C. 5.5 gives examples of allowable temporary services by an out-of-state attorney (e.g., meetings with the client, interviews of potential witnesses, and the review of documents) and explicitly omits from allowable 'temporary services' the signing and/or filing of any pleadings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if Rule 5.5 allows certain temporary services, it does not permit an out-of-state attorney to sign or file pleadings or to establish a systematic presence. Local court rules may permit appearance/signing only if accompanied by a proper application for pro hac vice admission. Establishing an office or continuous presence in the jurisdiction for practice is prohibited (Mass. R. Prof’l Conduct 5.5(b)(1)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pro hac vice admission cannot be presumed without application
rubrics_metrics.description: No pro hac vice admission will be offered by the court without an attorney first requesting it; it is unreasonable to expect admission without having sought it and satisfied prerequisites such as recruiting local counsel and filing necessary supporting documentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Routine grant of such motions assumes the applicant has met procedural prerequisites. A claim that pro hac vice admission was 'pending' is unsupported if the practitioner never filed the motion or did not demonstrate diligent efforts to obtain local counsel. Lack of evidence of 'diligent effort' to find local counsel precludes finding the expectation reasonable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishing 'temporary' practice cannot be stretched to multiple cases/continuous presence
rubrics_metrics.description: An out-of-state attorney's practice in the jurisdiction is not 'temporary' if he has appeared in multiple cases over multiple years or maintained an office or continuous presence; such sustained activity cannot be deemed temporary under the rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated appearances (e.g., appearing since 2005 in multiple matters), maintaining a law office, or representing multiple clients in more than one litigation while domiciled in the jurisdiction demonstrate a systematic and continuous presence inconsistent with 'temporary' practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(a) — disreputable or gross misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: '[A] practitioner shall not engage in disreputable or gross misconduct.' Disreputable conduct has generally included 'unprofessional' conduct and . . . 'any conduct violative of the ordinary standard of professional obligation and honor.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PTO/tribunal may rely on case law (e.g., Poole) and prior PTO proceedings. Examples include conduct that tends to bring the profession into disrepute or lessen public confidence in the profession. Engaging in unauthorized practice of law before a court (appearing/practicing without admission) is characterized as disreputable/gross misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(4) — dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation
rubrics_metrics.description: '[A] practitioner shall not engage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violations include presenting oneself as a licensed attorney while not authorized, representing pro hac vice admission as 'pending' when no motion was filed, using another attorney’s identification number, or otherwise making false/misleading statements about admission status. Case examples: Stemper, Corbin, Thornsberry, Stuligross. Signing pleadings and indicating pro hac vice pending without filing shows misrepresentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(5) — conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice
rubrics_metrics.description: '[A] practitioner shall not engage in conduct that is prejudicial to the administration of justice.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This covers conduct that negatively impacts the public’s perception or the efficacy of the courts or legal profession, or that hampers efficient and proper operation of courts or ancillary systems. Examples: inadequate representation, failure to appear, failure to communicate, failure to prosecute, or acting in ways that impede court functions. Practicing without authorization and ignoring court directives to obtain admission are prejudicial.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.77(b) — adequate preparation required
rubrics_metrics.description: '[A] practitioner shall not handle a legal matter without preparation adequate in the circumstances.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inadequate preparation is judged case-by-case and may be more likely where the violation involved willfulness (deliberate, intentional conduct). The tribunal may consider whether the attorney was put on notice to comply (e.g., prior admonitions) and nonetheless proceeded, indicating willful inadequate preparation (see Halvonik, Lopez).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.84(a)(1) — use of lawful means to seek client's objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: '[A] practitioner shall not intentionally fail to seek the lawful objectives of a client through reasonably available means permitted by law and the Disciplinary Rules.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pursuing client objectives through unlawful means (e.g., litigating in a forum without authorization to practice there) constitutes a violation. Failure to use available lawful means such as obtaining proper admission precludes lawfully prosecuting a client's case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unbundled/limited-scope ('ghostwriting') services do not permit unauthorized practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'unbundling' of legal services (providing limited tasks rather than full representation) is permitted when authorized, but it presumes the attorney is authorized to practice in the jurisdiction; unbundling does not allow an unlicensed attorney to draft and file pleadings or otherwise practice without admission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ABA Formal Opinion 07-446 describes unbundling as a lawyer performing only specific, limited tasks. Ghostwriting or preparing documents for pro se litigants might be permissible if the attorney is authorized, but not if the attorney is practicing without admission; unbundled services cannot be used as a cloak for unauthorized practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of 'diligent effort' required when claiming inability to find local counsel
rubrics_metrics.description: When a practitioner claims he could not find local counsel (to support a claim that admission pro hac vice was not possible), he must produce evidence depicting the 'diligent effort' he undertook to find such counsel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absent concrete evidence of effort, assertions that it was 'virtually impossible' or that counsel could not be found are insufficient to show a reasonable expectation of admission; tribunals will reject conclusory statements without supporting proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior admonition/notice increases culpability for continuing unauthorized practice
rubrics_metrics.description: An attorney who has been put on notice by a court or prior proceedings that he is required to seek pro hac vice admission (or not practice) and nevertheless continues to practice without admission demonstrates willfulness and increased culpability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior warnings (e.g., pre-Babeu) make subsequent similar conduct less defensible and support findings of willful misconduct, inadequate preparation, misrepresentation, and prejudice to the administration of justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court discretion and independence in admitting attorneys
rubrics_metrics.description: Admission before the Bar traditionally is considered subject to control by the admitting court, and this control is subject to review only for abuse of discretion or constitutional infirmities (Panzardi-Alvarez).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State bar or model rules do not override the admitting court’s local rules; compliance with a state's ethics rule alone does not satisfy a federal district court’s local admission requirements. Courts will not routinely admit applicants who have not satisfied local procedural prerequisites.
